# **Abstract** {#abstract}

The course “Data and Service Design: Designing Data-centric Services” intends to be a fundamental introduction to the notion of data for product-service system design students, providing them with conceptual and critical tools, as well as practice-oriented approaches and methods, to engage and work with data as a “material” in their design processes.

The understanding of the contemporary data landscape and its main topics will be developed through a double-track approach in which theoretical content and practical hands-on activities are carried out alongside each other.

# **1\. Introduction: Why Should We Care About Data?** {#1.-introduction:-why-should-we-care-about-data?}

Data has become a transversal concept for understanding how contemporary digital societies function. Whether concrete or simply perceived as such, the notion of data exerts an undoubtedly strong influence that appears ubiquitous, spanning economic, institutional, and cultural spheres. Most telling in this regard is how data has become part of public debate. Perhaps also due to several scandals in the tech world that gained international attention, even the non-technical layperson has grown accustomed to considering it normal that private and public organizations harness vast quantities of data.

Digital data of various typologies and from multiple sources has become a central asset for business optimization (e.g., Business Intelligence and Business Analytics) and the object of specific policies at national and supranational levels (e.g., the EU Data Act). Businesses and service providers collect data from internal routine activities (e.g., administrative work) and from their digital products and services (e.g., by monitoring touchpoints with users). Whether we support or criticise it, data collection and exploitation are now intrinsically part of how organizations operate and design and deliver their services and products across B2C industries (e.g., entertainment, mobility), B2B sectors (e.g., logistics, energy), and public services (e.g., welfare, healthcare, taxation).

For the field of product-service system design, data becomes relevant as design practitioners must understand how data is embodied in the design of product-service systems. This is especially true as data-driven features (e.g., analytics and user profiling) in these systems become entangled with semi-automated or algorithmic agencies — which the public discourse often generally labels as “Artificial Intelligence”. Failure to recognize bias in data or design choices may lead to economic and social damage, as it happened in the [Robodebt Scheme in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robodebt_scheme), [childcare benefits in the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_childcare_benefits_scandal), the [surge in Uber prices as people fled Hurricane Katrina](https://www.aiaaic.org/aiaaic-repository/ai-algorithmic-and-automation-incidents/uber-surge-pricing-criticised-as-people-flee-hurricane-sandy), or [racist labels due to a biased dataset in content recognition algorithms](https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-33347866). Data literacy also concerns the everyday practices and processes of design: it means being capable of engaging and working with data, whether originating from existing product-service systems or from available sources that help research and describe them.

Product-service system designers are accountable for what happens at the intersection of digital infrastructures, their automation, organizational strategies, existing regulations, and ethical concerns. They should develop their own critical capacity to navigate all these socio-technical dimensions while keeping into account value co-creation, therefore thinking within and beyond the systems they design for.

# **2\. Course perspective: Key Useful Concepts and Principles** {#2.-course-perspective:-key-useful-concepts-and-principles}

Any course is a collective learning journey. We seek to build a common vocabulary and perspective toward the topic addressed: data and service design.  
In line with this, we propose two concepts:

## **Data-Centric Services**  {#data-centric-services}

Several organizations find themselves in the position of being data holders: as a by-product of their activities, they possess relevant data that can potentially be turned into value. However, effectively utilizing this data requires addressing significant barriers, including interoperability, accessibility, management, and representation, while also ensuring compliance with legal and technical frameworks.

The concept of data-centric services (Leoni et al., 2023)— as opposed to data-driven services — emphasises the importance of designing services by leveraging data generated across different organizations and their information systems, which is often not yet linked, collected, or used consistently. Product-service system designers can engage with these scattered data sources by bringing a perspective that is useful for making sense of them and creating value from them, while supporting data holders in their sense-making processes and in building inter-organizational data governance and partnerships.

## **Data practices** {#data-practices}

Future designers should acknowledge data not as a neutral entity, but as something situated within service systems and carrying strong democratic and ethical implications (Falk, 2023\) — what is usually discussed under the label of data ethics. To recognise and critically address the contextual (social, political, organisational and material) conditions of data, theory alone is not sufficient: data must be engaged with in practice.

The concept of data practices for acknowledging data’s non-neutral and biased nature. In contrast to data as abstracted entities, practice compels students (as well as researchers) to recognise data as something always actively made by someone or something (Burkhardt et al., 2022). Actively working with data helps to outline issues that go beyond service systems. For example: Is my data collection publicly acceptable? Are all populations equally represented in my data? What might be the ultimate effects of this data on users and beyond?

Together, these two concepts define the perspective the course adopts toward the topic. The three resulting guiding principles of our journey are:

* Data is a central element of contemporary society  
* Data is contextual and inherently non-neutral  
* Data is a material for product-service system designing

*References:*

* *Burkhardt, M., van Geenen, D., Gerlitz, C., Hind, S., Kaerlein, T., Lämmerhirt, D. & Volmar, A. (2022). Interrogating Datafication: Towards a Praxeology of Data. Bielefeld: transcript Verlag. [https://doi.org/10.1515/9783839455616](https://doi.org/10.1515/9783839455616)*  
* *Leoni, F., Carraro, M., McAuliffe, E., & Maffei, S. (2023). Data-centric public services as potential source of policy knowledge. Can “design for policy” help?. Transforming Government: People, Process and Policy, 17(3), 399-411. [https://doi.org/10.1108/TG-06-2022-0088](https://doi.org/10.1108/TG-06-2022-0088)*  
* *Falk, P. (2023). Data matter: as data become matter, design matters. In The Materials of Service Design (pp. 143-148). Edward Elgar Publishing.*

# **3\. Approach: Learning Framework, Goals and Outputs** {#3.-approach:-learning-framework,-goals-and-outputs}

Given this perspective, the course unfolds through a *double-track approach* developed in parallel, during the course.*![][image4]*

## **Theoretical track** {#theoretical-track}

Primarily based on lectures by professors and guest speakers, it first introduces interpretative lenses that use “data” as a way to describe the contemporary world. It then focuses on the relationship between data and services, and from there discusses broader governance and ethical implications.

| Learning GoalDevelop a critical understanding of the contemporary data landscape and its main topics, referring them to the field of product-service system design. Understand the data, socio-technical, and organizational infrastructures. Relate theoretical concepts to their design choices. | Learning Outputs Understand and critically discuss the key concepts addressed in class and in the course bibliography. |
| :---- | :---- |

## **Practical track** {#practical-track}

Sequential and based on hands-on work in class: at each lesson, students will build upon what was done previously. This track is structured around three stages:

### PT Stage 1: Data-driven research and discovery

It will focus on the basics of accessing and manipulating heterogeneous data sources, such as those available from the web and social media. 

| Learning GoalCollecting data from various online sources (either through Open Data portals or by looking at other online sources), | Learning Outputs Understanding data types and structures Accessing and interpreting the most common type of data |
| :---- | :---- |

### PT Stage 2: Data modeling, preparation, and insight generation

Focuses on manipulating data into structured, analyzable formats and on developing appropriate data models to support exploration and analysis.

| Learning GoalTranslate analytical results into meaningful insights that can inform design decisions. Structure and model datasets, prepare data for analysis, and apply analytical techniques to generate and interpret insights relevant to service design challenges. | Learning Outputs Structuring, modeling, preparing, and integrating data to support analysis and exploration Identifying patterns, relationships, and trends to support insight generation |
| :---- | :---- |

### PT Stage 3: Data-driven representations

Focuses on how to work with data from a representational perspective, and on the methods and tools that can be used to visualize complex data in ways that support exploration and decision-making.

| Learning GoalDevelop data visualizations and use data representation methods to engage different audiences (e.g., other designers, users, and clients/stakeholders) throughout the design process. | Learning Outputs Develop data visualization skills and techniques Construct representations based on available data that can inform new service concepts  Integrate data representations with other sources to develop insights on services |
| :---- | :---- |

# **4\. Course Activities** {#4.-course-activities}

Given this framework, during the course, the class will engage with three main types of activities:

## **Lectures**

Theoretical classes addressing the topics covered in the course, followed by in-class discussions. These lectures introduce the topics that will be the focus of the final exam colloquium on the official exam date (see *7\. Evaluation*).

## **Guest lectures**

Presentations by experts on inspirational topics, specific themes, and case studies relevant to the intersection of data and product-service system design. Guest lectures are considered an integral part of the teaching programme; therefore, topics they address may be included in the final examination.

## **Classroom Practice**

Guided hands-on on specific data-driven methods and tools.   
For each practice, the class will work on a given practical example to be executed in class and linked to the Final Assignment. 

In-class work will be conducted using [Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/), a cloud-based Jupyter Notebook environment that allows writing and executing Python code directly in the browser without local configuration. In particular, students will use Colab to load and annotate datasets, clean and manipulate data, perform exploratory analysis, and develop visualizations.

Colab will serve not only as the technical tool for coding, but also as the structured learning environment for the course. Through a sequence of notebooks organized into thematic chapters corresponding to different classroom practices, students will progressively explore key concepts and methods. Each notebook will combine explanatory text, commented code, and short exercises.

The Colab notebooks provided by the instructor will function as templates and methodological references: students will be able to copy relevant portions of code, adapt them, and refine them according to the specific needs of their own case study  (see also *6\. Assignments*).

***Please make sure you can access this tool online through your Google Account.***

# **5\. Classroom Organization and Rules** {#5.-classroom-organization-and-rules}

The class will be divided into groups of max 7 people. Students are asked to work in groups for peer-to-peer support: you will be working on the same typologies of data and are encouraged to discuss them. However, note that *even if the Class Assignment is going to be developed and delivered in groups, your final score will be individual* (see *6\. Assignments*). To better coordinate the work, a Spokesperson for each team will be indicated as the interface between the groups and the professors. Given the large class size, students are required to consider some basic rules for working together and stay in the class:

## **Punctuality** 

Lessons start at 9.30 am. Please be punctual in the morning, respect breaks, and the lesson agenda.  The morning class is between 9:30 am and 1 pm, and the afternoon class is between 2:30 pm and 6 pm.

## **Signing the register (Attendants)**

**For each attendant student, signing the attendance register is mandatory twice a day**: in the morning (9:00–9:30 am) and in the afternoon (2:00–2:30 pm). The Teaching Assistant will oversee this task and should be considered the referee for it.  
We ask you to strictly respect the time of signing: outside these time slots, signing will not be allowed. Students not signing the register will be considered absent for the respective morning or afternoon. A total of **more than 2 days total of unrecorded attendance** will automatically result in the student being considered as a Non-Attendant (see *7\. Evaluation and Final Exam* for what this implies).

## **Attitude in class**

Reach out to professors and the teaching assistant when in doubt — there’s no such thing as a bad question. It is good to take an active role in discussions, activities, and individual exercises: it helps the class and fosters collective learning. Please, show courtesy to classmates, faculty, and guest speakers by listening attentively and participating constructively.

# **6\. Class Assignment: Critical Data Notebook** {#6.-class-assignment:-critical-data-notebook}

The course requires one main assignment that represents the final outcome of the in-class hands-on activities (see *3\. Approach* and *4\. Course Activities*). 

## **Assignment Description**

The main deliverable of this course is a **Critical Data Notebook** — a reflective and analytical journal developed progressively throughout the course through Colab. 

The objective of such a Notebook is to develop a documented and reflective output emerging from group data practices (analysis and visualization).   
The mixed text-and-code format of a Colab Notebook allows students to critically document their reasoning, choices, and learning process alongside their code used to explore, analize and visualize the data.

Students will work on broad **design opportunity areas** inspired by urban and territorial challenges contextualised in the areas of the **Municipality of Milan** and **Lombardy Region** (e.g., areas such as transportation, environment, and tourism). Starting from the analysis of available data on these contexts and their services, students are expected to ideate a basic *service concept* — an original idea for a service — or a re-design of an existing one. To achieve this, **a starting set of datasets** by Regione Lombardia[^1] will be provided by professors. Additional data sources and APIs will be introduced and discussed during the first lesson. Students are encouraged to further integrate these datasets during the course with other data and sources that could help them in reinforcing the analysis for this Assignment.

The Critical Notebook will be developed by working on the following analytical components that will be presented during the classroom practices and ideally represent “parts” that should be included in students’ notebooks. Such components are:

* Python 101 (numpy, pandas, matplotlib) and basic use of APIs  
* Dataset exploration and aggregation  
* Data manipulation & preparation, including introductory statistical techniques  
* Querying data and developing data visualizations

## **Assignment Delivery**

We will work on each module during the different lessons, so that the students will be guided in developing their final assignment by working step-by-step in class.

**Delivery of the assignment is mandatory to pass the course**, as it constitutes the main component of the final evaluation (see *7\. Evaluation*).   
The final deliverable is due on **May 7th** (one month after the end of the course) and will be discussed individually by each student on the final exam day.

Assignment delivery requirements and evaluation vary for Attending and Non-attending students (see also *7\. Evaluation*). Attending students will work in groups, while Non-attending students will work and deliver autonomously. Since Non-attending students will not collaborate with peers nor present their work during classes, they will receive fewer points for this activity. For Non-attending students, the same delivery structure and content requirements apply.

## **Assignment Presentation**

Attending students are required to present their work-in-progress to the faculty and the class on the last day of the course (April 9th). Non-attending students are exempt from this requirement.

The presentation should **effectively communicate** to the audience the service concept the group is developing, the analytical choices made, and the key insights emerging from the data. Rather than live-walking through the Notebook, students are expected to prepare a slide deck that may include relevant excerpts, visualizations, or outputs extracted from their Notebook.

The presentation will be evaluated on the ability to communicate clearly and effectively to a mixed audience — conveying both the analytical process and the conceptual direction of the service being identified.

# **7\. Evaluation** {#7.-evaluation}

The **final evaluation is individual** for each student and is based on the combined assessment of: 1\. the Class Assignment and 2\. the Exam Colloquium.   
The *Class Assignment* constitutes the majority of the final grade.   
Its evaluation will focus on:

A. The quality of the submitted Critical Data Notebook, assessed on:

* the appropriateness of the data choices and how representative they are of the challenge addressed;  
* the quality and clarity of the analysis and visualizations produced;  
* the coherence between the data analysis and the service concept developed;  
* the quality of the critical and reflective writing that complements the code.

B. The in-class presentation (Attending students only), assessed on the ability to communicate clearly and effectively to a mixed audience — conveying both the analytical process and the conceptual direction of the service being developed.

The *Exam Colloquium* accounts for the remaining portion of the evaluation. During the exam session, students will be assessed on:  
A. their knowledge of the course topics and concepts (as discussed during lectures) and their ability to critically discuss them with specific reference to the course bibliography. Each student will be asked to select 1 topic and 1 or 2 related readings from the Bibliography as starting topic to be discussed during the Exam Colloquium (additional topics may be asked by professors). Bibliography will be shared after first lesson and updated after each lesson.  
Further, the students will be evaluated on B. their ability to relate the theoretical discussion to the work developed for the Class Assignment.

See the table below for the weighting of each evaluation component.

|  | 1\. Class Assignment  |  | 2\. Exam Colloquium |  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **What is evaluated?** | A. Quality of Assignment Delivered (Critical Data Notebook)  | B. Capacity of presenting the in-progress Assignment as Group | A. Knowledge and critical discussion of topics/concepts with reference to the bibliography | B. Capacity of discussing theory in relation to Class Assignment |
| **Attendants** | Max 60% | Max 5% | Max 30% | Max 5% |
| **Non-attendants** | Max 50% | x | Max 40% | Max 10% |

**8\. Final Exam**

The final exam is organized as an individual colloquium with one of the two professors.

The whole class will be encouraged to select one common exam date among the available sessions, in order to complete all examinations on the same day and ensure greater consistency in evaluation. However, this remains a preferred option, and each student retains the right to register for any of the other scheduled sessions.

If a student decides to reject the grade proposed by the professor, the Class Assignment cannot be revised or resubmitted. The student may attend a subsequent exam session (if available) to improve the overall grade, but only the Exam Colloquium component of the evaluation can be reassessed.

# **8\. AI Tools Usage Policy for the Course** {#8.-ai-tools-usage-policy-for-the-course}

This course recognizes the value of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) as resources for enhancing research, exploring ideas, coding, and improving writing form. Students are encouraged to use these tools responsibly and ethically to support their learning process. Guidelines on how to properly and responsibly use AI tools, including effective prompting techniques and best practices, will be provided to students during the practice portion of the class.

**Prohibited Use of AI Tools**

Delivering written part of the Class Assignment that are entirely generated by AI is strictly prohibited. Submitting AI-generated content without personal contribution or critical reflection undermines the academic integrity of this course.

**Academic Integrity Measures**

* The faculty will employ plagiarism checker tools to verify the originality of submitted work.  
* If substantial plagiarism is detected, students may:  
  * Be asked to redo the assignment under closer supervision.  
  * Face further consequences in alignment with the university’s academic integrity policies.

Guidance on Responsible AI Use. Students are encouraged to:

* Use AI tools as a supplement, not a substitute, for their own research, writing, and critical thinking.  
* Properly credit sources and cite any material (AI-generated or otherwise) that contributes to their work.  
* Maintain transparency by indicating if AI tools were used to refine or assist with their writing.

By adhering to these guidelines, students can explore the benefits of AI tools while maintaining academic integrity and fostering genuine learning.

# **10\. Guest Lecturers** {#10.-guest-lecturers}

## **Andrea Benedetti**

Lecture (26th February)  
**Data and service: designing in (un)desired futures**

PhD in Design, Andrea Benedetti is currently UX/UI Designer at Università La Statale di Milano. His work revolves around using data to communicate invisible and complex issues.

## **Chiara Criscuolo**

Lecture (5th March)  
**Ethical Data Science: Challenges in a Responsible Innovation**

Chiara Criscuolo is currently a Data Scientist at the Bank of Italy, where she has been working since August 2023\. From 2021 to 2024, she served as a Research Fellow at Politecnico di Milano. In March 2025, she will defend her Ph.D. in Information Technology at Politecnico di Milano, with a focus on Ethical Data Science. She has taught several courses in both Italian and English at the bachelor's and master’s levels. Her research interests lie in Data Science, with particular emphasis on Data Quality, Data Mining, and the application of these methodologies to issues in Data Ethics.

## **Davide Posillipo**

Lecture (12th March)  
**Service Design and Data Engineering: an alliance towards impacts**

Davide Posillipo is a Scientist with a background in Statistics. He explores the intersection between Data, Design and Ethics. After more than a decade of hands-on experience in the data industry, he co-founded Komebi Studio, a company focused on designing and developing data intensive applications and AI features through the lenses of design and social awareness.

## **Federico Bartolomucci**

Lecture (19th March)  
**Using data for good: opportunities and challenges in the era of AI**

Federico is a Junior Assistant Professor in Management Engineering at Politecnico di Milano, within the TIRESIA Research group. His research is currently focusing on the intersection of social innovation, innovation ecosystems, and data. He teaches in multiple courses among with the course on Social Entrepreneurship, the Sustainable and Social Innovation Lab in the MSc degree on Management Engineering. He is adjunct professor at the Polimi Graduate School of Management. He is associate editor of the Data\&Policy journal. He has been co-chair of the Special Group created by the EU Commission on the Code of Conduct for Data Sharing and Use in the Social Economy.

## **Petter Falk**

Lecture (2nd April)  
**Data and/in democracy. Power, governance and value in data-driven public services**

Dr. Petter Falk is a senior lecturer in political science at Karlstad University, and also holds a position as a researcher in Media and Communication studies at Södertörn University, Stockholm.

## **Monica Vitali**

Lecture (9th April)  
**The hidden environmental cost of Data Management**

Associate Professor at the Department of Electronics, Information and Bioengineering (DEIB) of Politecnico di Milano, PhD in Information Technology.   
Her research focuses on the evaluation and management of energy efficiency and quality of service in information systems. Her work investigates new strategies to improve the efficiency of data centers, cloud and fog computing by applying techniques derived from the fields of artificial intelligence and machine learning.
